title: Vasquez: Trent allows fearing, not doubting; the just must absolutely believe they are in grace for the sacraments
source_text: XXVII. Haec manifeste colliguntur ex iis quae jam ex Vega, Stapletono, & ipso Bellarmino retulimus, ubi docent fideles & justos non oportere suspensos, dubios & anxios esse circa hoc an sint in Dei gratia, & ab iis alienam esse ejusmodi fluctuationem & haesitationem; adeoque qui sunt inter illos perfectiores, eo ipso habere pleniorem & firmiorem de propria gratia & justitia persuasionem. Sed praeterea diserte & expresse fatentur Theologi Scholae Romanae, justos de sua justificatione non posse dubitare, si prudenter se gerant; imo debere illos absolute credere se esse in gratia, si velint ea operari ad quae requiritur gratia, ut videre est apud Vasquezium, disp. pluries allegata, cap. 8. Observa, inquit, non dixisse Concilium quemlibet de sua gratia dubitare posse, sed de sua gratia timere posse, quod idem est atque formidare; omnis autem formido sine dubitatione oppositae partis esse potest. Dubitatio enim est haesitatio intellectus inter utramque partem contradictionis, ita ut in neutra parte ei appareat convenientia extremorum inter se, in cujus cognitione assensus consistit. Quamvis autem justus non sit dubius de sua justitia, quinimo sine dubio debeat absolute credere se esse in gratia, si velit aliqua operari ad quae requiritur gratia, ut administrationem & receptionem Sacramentorum; tamen etiam cum hoc absoluto assensu potest habere formidinem de sua justitia, &c. Cum igitur dicimus quemlibet justum de sua justificatione posse prudenter formidare, non intelligimus posse dubitare, si prudenter se gerat, & de neutra parte contradictionis judicare.
pass_a_gloss: These things are manifestly gathered from what we have already reported from Vega, Stapleton, and Bellarmine himself, where they teach that the faithful and just ought not to be suspended, doubtful, and anxious about whether they are in God’s grace, and that fluctuation and hesitation of that sort is foreign to them; and therefore that those who are more perfect among them thereby have a fuller and firmer persuasion concerning their own grace and righteousness. But besides, the theologians of the Roman School expressly confess that the just cannot doubt concerning their justification if they conduct themselves prudently; indeed that they ought absolutely to believe they are in grace if they wish to perform those things for which grace is required, as may be seen in Vasquez, in the disputation often alleged, chapter 8. Observe, he says, that the Council did not say that anyone can doubt concerning his grace, but that he can fear concerning his grace, which is the same as to dread; but every fear can exist without doubt of the opposite side. For doubt is a hesitation of the intellect between both sides of the contradiction, so that on neither side does the fitting of the extremes appear to it, in knowledge of which assent consists. But although the just person is not doubtful of his righteousness—nay rather without doubt he ought absolutely to believe he is in grace if he wishes to perform some things for which grace is required, as the administration and reception of the sacraments—yet even with this absolute assent he can have fear concerning his righteousness, etc. When therefore we say that any just person can prudently fear concerning his justification, we do not understand that he can doubt, if he conducts himself prudently, and judge concerning neither side of the contradiction.
pass_b_english: Roman authorities insist the prudent just must not live in suspended doubt about grace.
Vasquez reads Trent as allowing fear, not doubt, and requires absolute belief one is in grace to use the sacraments.
